title: Bruised Apple Detector
story: An orchard's packing line has a camera that flags apples it thinks are bruised. Most apples are fine, so a detector that never flags anything would be right most of the time, and useless.

Checking a test batch by hand, the orchard wants two honest numbers: of the flagged apples, how many were really bruised? Of the bruised apples, how many were caught? Plus one score balancing both. These are the standard scores for any yes/no classifier, from spam filters to medical screening.
task: Write detectorScores(flagged, bruised). flagged[i] is the camera's answer for apple i, and bruised[i] is the truth. Count:

• TP: flagged and bruised.
  • FP: flagged but fine.
  • FN: not flagged but bruised.
Return [precision, recall, f1] where precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / (TP + FN), and f1 = 2 · precision · recall / (precision + recall).
Whenever a denominator is 0, that score is 0. Empty lists give [0, 0, 0].
constraints: Each value is true or false.
Answers within 0.000001 of the expected values are accepted.

examples.explanation: Apples 0 and 4 are caught (TP = 2), apple 1 is a false alarm (FP = 1), apple 3 is missed (FN = 1). Precision 2 / 3, recall 2 / 3, so f1 is also 2 / 3.

Flagging everything catches the one bruised apple: recall 1. But only 1 of 4 flags was right: precision 0.25. f1 = 2 · 0.25 · 1 / 1.25 = 0.4, far below the plain average 0.625. F1 drops sharply when either score is poor.
Nothing was flagged. TP + FP = 0, so precision is 0 by the rule, and recall is 0 / 1 = 0. So f1 is 0 too.

hints: In the second example the camera flagged every apple and caught every bruised one. Is it a good detector? Which of the story's two questions exposes it?
Every apple lands in one of four boxes: caught, false alarm, missed, or correctly ignored. Which boxes do precision and recall use?
Precision divides by everything flagged (TP + FP). Recall divides by everything really bruised (TP + FN). Correctly ignored apples are in neither.
One loop counts TP, FP and FN. Then compute the three scores, checking each denominator for 0 first. F1 is the harmonic mean, not the plain average.
bruteForce: You could build lists of flagged and bruised positions and intersect them to find TP. It works, but it is more machinery than needed.

The real trap is accuracy (correct answers over all apples): when few apples are bruised, a camera that never flags scores high while catching nothing. Counting the three boxes in one pass gives the honest scores.

js: * @param {boolean[]} flagged  the camera's verdict per apple
py: def detector_scores(flagged: list[bool], bruised: list[bool]) -> list[float]:

tests.note: single fine apple, all denominators zero
lazy detector: high accuracy, zero recall

js: if (flagged[i] && bruised[i]) tp++;       // caught a bad apple
else if (!flagged[i] && bruised[i]) fn++; // missed a bad apple
const precision = tp + fp === 0 ? 0 : tp / (tp + fp);
const recall = tp + fn === 0 ? 0 : tp / (tp + fn);
const f1 = precision + recall === 0 ? 0 : (2 * precision * recall) / (precision + recall);
py: for f, b in zip(flagged, bruised):
precision = 0.0 if tp + fp == 0 else tp / (tp + fp)
recall = 0.0 if tp + fn == 0 else tp / (tp + fn)
walkthrough: Sort every apple into a box; each score is a ratio of box counts. Correctly ignored apples (TN) never appear, which is why these scores are not fooled by a mostly fine batch.
Trace flagged = [T, T, F, F, T, F], bruised = [T, F, F, T, T, F]:
• Apple 2: not flagged, fine. No box needed.
Precision = 2 / 3, recall = 2 / 3, f1 = 2 · (2/3) · (2/3) / (4/3) = 2 / 3. When precision and recall are equal, F1 equals them; otherwise it sits closer to the smaller one.
solution.timeWhy: One pass to count the boxes.
solution.takeaway: For yes/no classifiers, count TP, FP and FN, then read off precision (how trustworthy a "yes" is), recall (how many real cases you catch) and F1 (their harmonic mean). Guard zero denominators, and distrust accuracy when one class is rare.
